lesson_title: Three Directions and a Sheet of Dots
hook_text: Up, up-right, up-left. That is all you need to draw anything in 3D so it can be measured.
clip_script: Here is how engineers draw in 3D. Three directions. Up is straight up. Width goes up to the right at 30 degrees. Depth goes up to the left at 30 degrees. Equal angles, equal treatment: isometric means equal measure. Now take dotted isometric paper, where the dots already run in those three directions. Start at a bottom corner. Count up for the height, up-right for the width, up-left for the depth. Three lines meeting. Close the front face, close the side, run the top edges back until they meet. A box. A frame is just thin boxes: a flat base parallelogram, four verticals, rails across, and the braces last, corner to corner, because diagonals are never true length. Write the real sizes along the edges, the scale in the corner. One picture that explains the whole design and can still be measured.
visual_style: Three axis lines fan out from a dot; a grid of dots appears; a box builds edge by edge; it becomes a braced frame with an axle; dimensions slope along the edges.
pacing: Axes in ten seconds, box in twenty, frame in twenty, dimensions to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and draw your PAT frame on isometric grid paper at 1:2.
